S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
examples: Makes mistakes in homework or tests by misreading questions or skipping important parts.
Frequently omits details or makes typos in work documents or reports.
Repeats mistakes in calculations or numerical work, such as switching signs or getting digits wrong.
Performs tasks incorrectly by missing important details in instructions.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention that interferes with functioning or development, with relatively fewer overt hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Individuals often struggle with sustaining focus, following through on tasks, organizing activities, and managing details, despite having normal intelligence and, at times, strong areas of interest-based performance. Symptoms usually begin in childhood, though many adults are diagnosed later when environmental demands exceed compensatory strategies, such as in complex jobs or changing life roles. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, and cognitive disorders by its early onset, chronic course, and consistent difficulties with attention and organization across settings, though it may be unmasked or exacerbated by stress or comorbid conditions.

patient.stressor: About a year ago, Thang was promoted to lead architect on a major AI-driven creative platform, shifting his role from primarily coding to coordinating distributed teams, integrating multiple codebases, and managing patent documentation. The increased volume of concurrent meetings, architectural decisions, and long-term planning made it harder for him to rely on the deep-focus coding sprints that had previously masked his longstanding attention difficulties. Over the following months, missed integration deadlines, overlooked requirements in design documents, and repeated rework on client-facing demos began to draw concern from his manager and frustration from junior developers he was mentoring. As these organizational demands started to spill over into forgotten workshop commitments and last-minute scrambles around travel and gallery submissions, Thang sought psychiatric evaluation after his annual review explicitly cited his growing difficulty keeping track of complex tasks and details.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can handle the technical parts fine, but I just can’t seem to keep all the pieces of these projects organized anymore.”

S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
S001.manifestation: In the last year my team has started double‑checking everything I write because I’ll miss a single parameter in an API call or skim past one line in a spec, and that tiny oversight turns into hours of rework even though I thought I’d been careful the first time through.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
S003.manifestation: In meetings people will say, ‘Thang, are you with us?’ because I’ll be staring at the slides but my brain has drifted off to thinking about a bug from this morning, and then I realize I have no idea what decision they just discussed and have to ask them to repeat it.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: Now that I’m supposed to juggle roadmaps, code reviews, patents, and client demos at the same time, it feels like my head is a messy whiteboard where everything is half‑erased, so I keep jumping between tasks without a clear order and end up scrambling the night before big milestones to pull it all together.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: It’s gotten almost comical how often I misplace essentials—my badge, notebook, even my laptop charger—so I’ll spend ten minutes before a stand‑up or a flight tearing through my backpack and desk drawers for something I’m sure I just had in my hand.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: When I try to sit down and review architecture documents, the slightest thing—a Slack notification, someone walking past the glass wall, or even a random thought about a painting idea—pulls me off the page, and ten minutes later I’m reading an unrelated article or sketching instead of finishing the review.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: On long Zoom calls where I’m mostly listening, I feel this restless buzz in my body, like I need to get up or do something with my hands, so I end up constantly shifting in my chair, pacing off‑camera, or opening new tabs just to burn off the feeling of being stuck.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
S013.manifestation: Even with things I enjoy, like reading sci‑fi or sketching concepts for the platform, I can’t seem to just sit quietly and immerse myself anymore—I’ll read the same paragraph three times, start talking out loud to myself about an unrelated idea, or put on a podcast because pure silence makes me antsy within minutes.
